questionBank.explanation: RS-232 (Recommended Standard 232) is an older serial communication standard that used a DB-9 or DB-25 connector to connect modems, printers, mice, and other peripheral devices. RJ11 is a telephone connector, and RG-6/RG-59 are coaxial cable types.

questionBank.stem: Thunderbolt 1 uses two separate 10 Gbps data channels, providing a combined maximum throughput of 20 Gbps. However, a single task may use only one of these channels at a time, limiting the speed to 10 Gbps per task. Thunderbolt 2 bonds the two channels into one unified 20 Gbps connection, allowing one high-bandwidth task to utilize the full capacity, while Thunderbolt 3 further increases this overall throughput to 40 Gbps.
questionBank.explanation: True. Thunderbolt 1 has two 10 Gbps channels used independently (10 Gbps per task), Thunderbolt 2 bonds them into a single 20 Gbps channel for one high-bandwidth task, and Thunderbolt 3 increases total throughput to 40 Gbps using the USB-C connector.

questionBank.stem: What is the maximum allowable length for a Thunderbolt copper cable?
questionBank.explanation: The maximum allowable length for a Thunderbolt copper cable is up to 3 meters. High-quality short cables (0.5m) achieve maximum performance, while longer passive copper cables may have reduced speeds.

questionBank.stem: The fiber-optic Thunderbolt interface allows for a maximum cable length of:
questionBank.explanation: Fiber-optic Thunderbolt cables allow a maximum length of 60 meters, far exceeding the 3-meter copper limit. The optical connection maintains full bandwidth over this longer distance.

questionBank.stem: Which of the following answers refer(s) to video connection standards? (Select all that apply)
questionBank.explanation: DVI, DisplayPort, HDMI, and VGA are all video connection standards designed to transmit video signals from a source to a display. SATA and eSATA are storage interfaces, and USB is a general-purpose peripheral interface (though USB-C can carry video via Alt Mode).

questionBank.stem: Which of the interfaces listed below provide the capability for transmission of both video and audio data? (Select 2 answers)
questionBank.explanation: HDMI and DisplayPort both transmit video and audio data over a single cable. DVI and VGA are video-only interfaces that do not carry audio signals. S/PDIF is an audio-only interface.

questionBank.stem: What are the characteristic features of the signal that can be carried through an HDMI cable? (Select 2 answers)
questionBank.explanation: HDMI carries a digital signal (not analog) and transmits both video and audio data through a single cable. This digital audio/video capability is one of HDMI's key advantages over older analog interfaces like VGA.

questionBank.stem: Which of the following answers best describes the signal capabilities of DisplayPort?
questionBank.explanation: DisplayPort carries digital audio and video signals. It supports high resolutions, high refresh rates, adaptive sync technologies (FreeSync/G-Sync), and can daisy-chain multiple monitors.

questionBank.stem: Which of the DVI versions listed below does not provide support for digital signal transmission?
questionBank.explanation: DVI-A (Analog) supports only analog signal transmission and does not provide digital signal support. DVI-D is digital-only, and DVI-I (Integrated) supports both analog and digital signals.

questionBank.stem: Which DVI type does not provide support for analog signal transmission?
questionBank.explanation: DVI-D (Digital) supports only digital signal transmission and does not provide analog support. DVI-A is analog-only, and DVI-I supports both analog and digital signals.

questionBank.stem: DVI-I provides support for both digital and analog video signal transmission.
questionBank.explanation: True. DVI-I (Integrated) supports both digital and analog video signal transmission through a single connector. The 'I' stands for Integrated, combining both DVI-D and DVI-A capabilities.

questionBank.stem: Which of the answers listed below refer to the characteristic features of the signal that can be carried through a standard VGA cable? (Select 2 answers)
questionBank.explanation: A standard VGA cable carries an analog video-only signal. VGA does not transmit audio or digital signals—it uses a 15-pin D-sub connector to send analog video from the source to the display.

questionBank.stem: USB-C supports Alternate Mode (Alt Mode), which allows it to transmit video signals using protocols such as DisplayPort or HDMI. Through Alt Mode, USB-C can deliver video to external displays like monitors or TVs, offering the same functionality as dedicated video cables. To connect to most external displays, USB-C requires a compatible adapter or cable, such as USB-C to DisplayPort or USB-C to HDMI.
questionBank.explanation: True. USB-C Alternate Mode (Alt Mode) allows the USB-C connector to carry non-USB protocols like DisplayPort or HDMI video signals, enabling video output to external displays. Compatible adapters or cables (USB-C to DisplayPort/HDMI) are typically needed to connect to standard display inputs.

questionBank.stem: What are the characteristic features of SATA revision 1.0 (SATA I)? (Select 2 answers)
questionBank.explanation: SATA revision 1.0 (SATA I) provides a 1.5 Gbps data transfer rate (approximately 150 MB/s) and has a maximum cable length of 1 meter. These are the baseline specifications that were doubled in subsequent SATA revisions.

questionBank.stem: The SATA interface specification defines a power connector consisting of:
questionBank.explanation: The SATA interface specification defines a 15-pin power connector that supplies 3.3V, 5V, and 12V DC power to storage devices. The separate 7-pin connector handles data only.

questionBank.stem: SATA revision 2.0 (SATA II) specifies: (Select 2 answers)
questionBank.explanation: SATA revision 2.0 (SATA II) provides a 3 Gbps data transfer rate (approximately 300 MB/s), double that of SATA I, while maintaining the same maximum cable length of 1 meter.

questionBank.stem: A single SATA data cable can be used to connect a motherboard slot with:
questionBank.explanation: A single SATA data cable connects only one device to one motherboard port—it is a point-to-point connection. Unlike older PATA/IDE cables that could support two devices (master/slave), SATA uses dedicated one-to-one connections.

questionBank.stem: The characteristic features of SATA revision 3.0 (SATA III) include: (Select 2 answers)
questionBank.explanation: SATA revision 3.0 (SATA III) provides a 6 Gbps data transfer rate (approximately 600 MB/s) and maintains the standard maximum cable length of 1 meter. This is currently the fastest SATA data transfer specification.

questionBank.stem: The SATA interface specification defines a data cable connector consisting of:
questionBank.explanation: The SATA interface defines a 7-pin data cable connector for data transfer between the motherboard and storage device. Power is supplied separately through the 15-pin SATA power connector.

questionBank.stem: Shares Which of the following answers refer(s) to eSATA? (Select all that apply)
questionBank.explanation: eSATA (external SATA) provides an external connection for storage devices, supports data transfer rates up to 6 Gbps (matching SATA III), has a standard cable length of up to 2 meters, and is hot-swappable. The 4 Gbps option is incorrect as eSATA matches SATA III at 6 Gbps, and the 1-meter limit applies to internal SATA cables.
options: Data transfer rate of up to 4 Gbps
A standard cable length of up to 2 meters
Data transfer rate of up to 6 Gbps
correctAnswer: A standard cable length of up to 2 meters
Data transfer rate of up to 6 Gbps

questionBank.stem: Which of the answers listed below describes the functionality offered by a cable adapter?
questionBank.explanation: A cable adapter adjusts the connector form factor from one type to another (e.g., HDMI to DVI, USB-A to USB-C) without changing the signal. It does not expand ports, amplify signals, or enable hot-swapping—those are functions of hubs, repeaters/extenders, and hot-swap controllers.
options: Hot swap capability for connected devices

questionBank.stem: Which of the following answer choices describe typical applications of the RJ11 connector? (Select 3 answers)
questionBank.explanation: RJ11 connectors are used with telephone equipment, dial-up networking (connecting to an analog modem), and twisted-pair copper cabling (typically two-pair). RJ11 is not used for Ethernet (which uses RJ45), fiber-optic, or coaxial cabling.

questionBank.stem: The RJ45 connector is used with: (Select 2 answers)
questionBank.explanation: RJ45 connectors are used with twisted-pair copper cabling and Ethernet network cabling. They terminate four-pair (8-wire) cables for network connections. RJ45 is not used with fiber, coax, dial-up, or telephone equipment (which uses RJ11).

questionBank.stem: What are the characteristic features of the F-type connector? (Select 3 answers)
questionBank.explanation: The F-type connector is a threaded (screw-on) coaxial connector used for satellite/cable TV and broadband Internet connections via cable modems. It uses coaxial cabling, not twisted-pair. The bayonet-style connector describes the BNC type, and professional audio/video/CCTV applications typically use BNC connectors.
options: Satellite/cable TV, broadband Internet connections via cable modems
Professional audio and video equipment, CCTV systems, laboratory, and testing equipment
correctAnswer: Satellite/cable TV, broadband Internet connections via cable modems

questionBank.stem: Examples of connector types used with fiber-optic cabling include: (Select all that apply)
questionBank.explanation: LC (Lucent Connector), ST (Straight Tip), and SC (Subscriber Connector) are all fiber-optic cable connector types. RCA is an analog audio/video connector, BNC is a coaxial connector, and XLR is a professional audio connector—none of these are fiber-optic.

questionBank.stem: A termination device (or module) that secures individual wires directly onto metal contacts to form permanent, solderless connections is known as:
questionBank.explanation: A punchdown block is a termination device that secures individual wires directly onto metal contacts using insulation displacement connectors (IDCs) to form permanent, solderless connections. It is used on the back of patch panels and wall jacks in structured cabling installations.

questionBank.stem: Which of the answers listed below refer(s) to (a) non-reversible connector type(s) used in older mobile devices? (Select all that apply)
questionBank.explanation: MicroUSB and MiniUSB are non-reversible connector types commonly found in older mobile devices. They can only be inserted one way. USB-C is the modern reversible connector, while USB Type-A and Type-B are primarily used on host/peripheral devices rather than mobile devices.

questionBank.stem: Which of the following answers applies to USB-C connector?
questionBank.explanation: USB-C features all of the listed capabilities: a symmetrical (reversible) connector design, bi-directional power and data transfer, video output via DisplayPort/HDMI Alt Mode, and high data transfer speeds (up to 40 Gbps with USB4/Thunderbolt).

questionBank.stem: What is the name of the most common connector type used for providing power to various hardware components inside a computer case?
questionBank.explanation: The Molex connector is the most common 4-pin power connector used inside computer cases to supply power to various hardware components like fans, older hard drives, and optical drives. It provides 5V and 12V DC power using color-coded wires.

questionBank.stem: Which of the answers listed below refers to a proprietary 8-pin connector used for charging, data transfer, and audio output in iOS devices?
questionBank.explanation: Lightning is Apple's proprietary 8-pin connector used in iOS devices (iPhones and iPads) for charging, data transfer, and audio output. FireWire and Thunderbolt are different interfaces, and Dock Connector was Apple's older 30-pin interface.

questionBank.stem: Which of the following answers refers to a serial communication copper connector often found on older PCs, networking equipment, and industrial hardware?
questionBank.explanation: The DB-9 (a 9-pin D-subminiature connector) is a serial communication connector associated with RS-232, commonly found on older PCs, networking equipment (console ports), and industrial hardware. PS/2 is for keyboards/mice, and RG-6/RG-59 are coaxial cable designations.

questionBank.stem: What is the most common memory module form factor used in laptops?
questionBank.explanation: SODIMM (Small Outline Dual Inline Memory Module) is the most common memory module form factor used in laptops and compact devices due to its smaller physical size. DIMMs are used in desktops, ECC RAM is an error-correcting type, and CRIMM is an obsolete RDRAM continuity module.

questionBank.stem: Which type of RAM features separate electrical contacts on each side of the module?
questionBank.explanation: A DIMM (Dual Inline Memory Module) features separate electrical contacts on each side of the module, making each side an independent connection. A SIMM (Single Inline Memory Module) has redundant contacts on both sides that carry the same signals. SRAM and DRAM are memory technologies, not form factors.

questionBank.stem: The placement of a notch on the RAM module contact surface ensures proper alignment of the module with the memory bank on the motherboard and prevents the installation of incompatible memory types.
questionBank.explanation: True. The notch (key) on a RAM module's contact surface is positioned differently for each DDR generation (DDR3, DDR4, DDR5), ensuring proper alignment with the motherboard slot and physically preventing installation of an incompatible memory type.

questionBank.stem: Which of the answers listed below refer(s) to the characteristic feature(s) of Static Random- Access Memory (SRAM)? (Select all that apply)
questionBank.explanation: SRAM (Static RAM) is faster than DRAM, more expensive than DRAM, volatile (loses data when power is removed), and is used for CPU cache memory. SRAM does not need constant refreshing like DRAM, which makes it faster but also more costly and lower density.
options: Widely used as the primary storage media (regular RAM modules installed in memory slots on the motherboard)
More expensive in comparison to Dynamic Random-Access Memory (DRAM)
Utilized for CPU cache memory chips
Less expensive in comparison to Dynamic Random-Access Memory (DRAM)
correctAnswer: More expensive in comparison to Dynamic Random-Access Memory (DRAM)
Utilized for CPU cache memory chips

questionBank.stem: Which of the following answers describes(s) the characteristics of Dynamic Random-Access Memory (DRAM)? (Select all that apply)
questionBank.explanation: DRAM (Dynamic RAM) is volatile, slower than SRAM, widely used as primary system memory (installed in motherboard slots), and less expensive than SRAM. DRAM stores data in capacitors that must be constantly refreshed, making it slower but cheaper and higher-density than SRAM.
options: Utilized for CPU cache memory chips
More expensive in comparison to Static Random-Access Memory (SRAM)
Widely used as the primary storage media (regular RAM modules installed in memory slots on the motherboard)
Less expensive in comparison to Static Random-Access Memory (SRAM)
correctAnswer: Widely used as the primary storage media (regular RAM modules installed in memory slots on the motherboard)
Less expensive in comparison to Static Random-Access Memory (SRAM)

questionBank.stem: The term "Synchronous Dynamic Random-Access Memory (SDRAM)" refers to a broad category of DRAM modules that rely on the signal sent by the system clock in order to coordinate their functioning with other internal PC components.
questionBank.explanation: True. SDRAM (Synchronous Dynamic RAM) is a broad category of DRAM that synchronizes its operations with the system clock signal, coordinating data transfers with other internal PC components for improved performance over older asynchronous DRAM.

questionBank.stem: SDRAM's backward compatibility feature provides a convenient way to build PCs using different types of SDRAM modules.
questionBank.explanation: False. SDRAM generations (DDR3, DDR4, DDR5) are not backward compatible with each other. Each generation has different pin counts, notch positions, voltages, and signaling, preventing modules from being installed in slots designed for a different DDR version.

questionBank.stem: Which of the answers listed below refers to a valid SDRAM module combination that can be installed on a single PC motherboard?
questionBank.explanation: None of the listed combinations are valid because DDR SDRAM generations are not backward compatible. DDR3, DDR4, and DDR5 each have different physical keying (notch positions), pin counts, and electrical specifications, so they cannot be mixed on a single motherboard.

questionBank.stem: Which of the following answers refer to the Double Data Rate 3 Synchronous Dynamic Random- Access Memory (DDR3 SDRAM)? (Select 3 answers)
questionBank.explanation: DDR3 SDRAM has 240 contact pins, a maximum capacity of 16 GB per module, and uses a keyed notch to prevent installation of incompatible memory types. DDR3 is not backward compatible with other DDR generations, and 288 pins and 32 GB capacity describe DDR4.
options: 16 GB maximum capacity per memory module
A notch on the RAM module contact surface prevents the installation of incompatible memory types
32 GB maximum capacity per memory module
Backwards compatible with earlier DDR SDRAM versions
correctAnswer: 16 GB maximum capacity per memory module
A notch on the RAM module contact surface prevents the installation of incompatible memory types

questionBank.stem: What are the characteristic features of the Double Data Rate 4 Synchronous Dynamic Random- Access Memory (DDR4 SDRAM)? (Select 3 answers)
questionBank.explanation: DDR4 SDRAM has 288 contact pins, a maximum capacity of 32 GB per module, and uses a keyed notch positioned differently from DDR3 to prevent incompatible installation. DDR4 is not backward compatible with DDR3 or DDR5, and 240 pins describe DDR3.
options: 32 GB maximum capacity per memory module
64 GB maximum capacity per memory module
A notch on the RAM module contact surface prevents the installation of incompatible memory types
Backwards compatible with earlier DDR SDRAM versions
correctAnswer: 32 GB maximum capacity per memory module
A notch on the RAM module contact surface prevents the installation of incompatible memory types

questionBank.stem: Which of the answers listed below refer to Double Data Rate 5 Synchronous Dynamic Random- Access Memory (DDR5 SDRAM)? (Select 3 answers)
questionBank.explanation: DDR5 SDRAM has 288 contact pins (same count as DDR4 but with a different notch position), supports up to 64 GB per module, and uses a keyed notch to prevent incompatible installation. DDR5 is not backward compatible with earlier DDR versions.
options: Backwards compatible with earlier DDR SDRAM versions
64 GB maximum capacity per memory module
A notch on the RAM module contact surface prevents the installation of incompatible memory types
32 GB maximum capacity per memory module
correctAnswer: 64 GB maximum capacity per memory module
A notch on the RAM module contact surface prevents the installation of incompatible memory types

questionBank.stem: Certain types of RAM use an additional bit to detect whether a data error has occurred. This extra bit stores information about the count of bits set to 1 in a given data string (typically one byte). Examining the value of this bit at different stages of processing allows for the detection of data corruption. What is the name of that extra bit?
questionBank.explanation: A parity bit is an extra bit added to data that stores whether the count of 1-bits in the data is odd or even. By comparing parity at different processing stages, single-bit data corruption can be detected. A checksum, digest, and CRC are more complex error-detection methods.

questionBank.stem: ECC type RAM:
questionBank.explanation: ECC (Error Correction Code) RAM can both detect and correct single-bit memory errors, preventing data corruption and system crashes. Unlike parity RAM (which can only detect errors), ECC uses additional bits and algorithms to identify and fix errors automatically.
options: Can only detect errors, but does not have the capability to correct them
Refers to parity RAM (the two terms are interchangeable)
Offers better performance in terms of speed when compared to a non-ECC type of RAM

questionBank.stem: Shares ECC RAM finds extensive use in environments where data integrity is essential, such as in critical infrastructure, high-availability systems, and applications requiring precise error detection and correction. It prioritizes data integrity over cost and performance, making it more expensive and slightly slower than non-ECC RAM in most cases.
questionBank.explanation: ECC (Error Correction Code) RAM detects and corrects single-bit memory errors and detects multi-bit errors, making it essential for servers and critical infrastructure where data integrity is paramount. It uses a 72-bit data bus (vs. standard 64-bit) for its checksum, making it more expensive and slightly slower than non-ECC RAM.

questionBank.stem: Which of the following characteristics apply to the type of RAM most commonly used as the main system memory in desktop PCs? (Select 2 answers)
questionBank.explanation: Desktop PCs most commonly use Dynamic RAM (DRAM), which stores data using capacitors that must be constantly refreshed, in full-size DIMM form factor. Consumer desktops use non-ECC memory because ECC RAM is more expensive and requires compatible motherboards/CPUs typically found in servers and workstations.

questionBank.stem: The color-coded memory slots on the motherboard indicate that a given motherboard provides support for the multi-channel memory architecture.
questionBank.explanation: Motherboards with multi-channel memory support use color-coded DIMM slots (e.g., matching blue and black pairs) to indicate which slots should be populated together. Installing matching modules in same-colored slots enables dual-channel, triple-channel, or quad-channel memory configurations for increased bandwidth.

questionBank.stem: Taking advantage of the performance benefits offered by the multi-channel memory architecture requires: (Select all that apply)
questionBank.explanation: Multi-channel memory requires modules of matching type, speed, and capacity installed in the correct color-matched slots on the motherboard. Installing modules in opposite-colored slots would place them on the same channel rather than enabling multi-channel operation, which defeats the purpose of the configuration.
options: Installing memory modules in slots of opposite color on the motherboard
Memory modules of the same capacity
Installing modules in appropriate memory slots (slots of matching color) on the motherboard
correctAnswer: Memory modules of the same capacity
Installing modules in appropriate memory slots (slots of matching color) on the motherboard

questionBank.stem: The platters in a magnetic hard drive spin at a rate measured in:
questionBank.explanation: HDD platters spin at a rate measured in revolutions per minute (RPM). Common HDD speeds include 5,400 RPM and 7,200 RPM for consumer drives, and up to 10,000 or 15,000 RPM for enterprise drives, with higher RPM generally providing faster data access.

questionBank.stem: What is the maximum RPM value available in modern HDDs?
questionBank.explanation: The maximum RPM available in modern HDDs is 15,000 RPM, found in enterprise-class SAS (Serial Attached SCSI) drives designed for servers and data centers where high-speed random access is critical.

questionBank.stem: Which of the answers listed below refers to a storage media drive form factor for laptop computers?
questionBank.explanation: The 2.5-inch form factor is the standard size for laptop storage drives, used for both HDDs and SSDs. This smaller form factor fits the space constraints of portable devices, compared to the 3.5-inch drives used in desktops.

questionBank.stem: Which of the following answers refers to an HDD form factor for desktops?
questionBank.explanation: The 3.5-inch form factor is the standard HDD size for desktop PCs, offering higher storage capacities than 2.5-inch drives. Desktop cases have dedicated 3.5-inch drive bays designed to accommodate these larger drives.

questionBank.stem: Which of the statements listed below can be used to describe the features of NVMe? (Select 2 answers)
questionBank.explanation: NVMe (Non-Volatile Memory Express) was developed specifically as a host controller interface for SSDs, replacing the older AHCI protocol designed for spinning drives. NVMe uses the PCIe interface for data transfer, providing significantly higher throughput and lower latency than SATA-based SSDs.
options: Uses the PCIe interface for data transfer
Capped at a maximum data transfer rate of 6 Gbps
Designed as a general-purpose interface for various hardware devices
correctAnswer: Uses the PCIe interface for data transfer

questionBank.stem: Which of the following answers does not apply to the SATA interface?
questionBank.explanation: The question asks which does NOT apply to SATA — since the answer is 'All of the above statements accurately describe the SATA interface,' all listed statements (7-pin data connector, hot-swappable, speeds up to 600 MBps for SATA III) are valid characteristics of the SATA interface.
options: Common in 2.5-inch SSDs replacing traditional HDDs
Widely used in consumer-grade laptops and desktops
An older interface originally designed for mechanical hard drives
Capped at a maximum data transfer rate of 6 Gbps
All of the above statements accurately describe the SATA interface
correctAnswer: All of the above statements accurately describe the SATA interface

questionBank.stem: PCIe is a general-purpose, high-speed interface that serves as the backbone for NVMe SSDs and other high-performance hardware devices.
questionBank.explanation: PCIe (PCI Express) is a high-speed, point-to-point serial interface that serves as the primary expansion bus in modern PCs. It provides dedicated bandwidth to each connected component and is used for graphics cards, NVMe SSDs, NICs, capture cards, and other expansion devices.

questionBank.stem: What are the key features of SAS? (Select 3 answers)
questionBank.explanation: SAS (Serial Attached SCSI) is designed for enterprise environments requiring high reliability, redundancy, and uptime. It supports daisy-chain topology for multi-drive configurations and is commonly found in servers and data centers where mission-critical data storage is essential.
options: Designed for systems requiring high redundancy, error correction, and uptime
Optimized for multi-drive configurations in a daisy-chain topology
Commonly implemented in mission-critical environments like servers and data centers
Widely used in 2.5-inch SSDs replacing traditional HDDs
Developed specifically for high-throughput, low-latency flash storage environments
correctAnswer: Designed for systems requiring high redundancy, error correction, and uptime
Optimized for multi-drive configurations in a daisy-chain topology
Commonly implemented in mission-critical environments like servers and data centers

questionBank.stem: An M.2 key is a notch on the pin contact surface of an M.2 expansion card which prevents its insertion into an incompatible socket. The 12 available M.2 key IDs are letters from A to M which indicate the location of notched pins on the card’s contact surface and designate the type of interface a given card is compatible with. M.2 expansion cards used for solid-state storage applications have key IDs of B and M. The B-keyed M.2 SSD cards take advantage of 2 lanes of a PCIe link (lower read/write speed), the M-keyed M.2 SSDs use 4 PCIe lanes (higher read/write speed). M.2 SSDs with 2 notches on the card’s pin contact surface (B + M) increase their compatibility, as they can be installed in either of the two types of expansion slots on the motherboard.
questionBank.explanation: An M.2 key is a notch on the connector edge of an M.2 card that determines physical and electrical compatibility with motherboard slots. Different key types (B key, M key, B+M key) correspond to different supported interfaces (SATA, PCIe x2, PCIe x4), preventing installation of incompatible cards.

questionBank.stem: Which of the answers listed below refers to an older, portable device SSD form factor superseded by M.2?
questionBank.explanation: mSATA (mini-SATA) is an older, compact SSD form factor designed for portable devices that predates the M.2 standard. It uses the SATA interface in a smaller card format and has been largely superseded by M.2 SSDs, which offer more flexibility and higher performance options.

questionBank.stem: Which of the following answers refer(s) to a standard form factor for SSDs? (Select all that apply)
questionBank.explanation: M.2 and mSATA are both standard SSD form factors that use compact card designs rather than traditional 2.5-inch drive enclosures. M.2 is the current standard supporting both SATA and NVMe interfaces, while mSATA is the older portable form factor using SATA only.

questionBank.stem: Hardware RAID Level 0: (Select all that apply)
questionBank.explanation: RAID 0 (disk striping) requires a minimum of 2 drives, splits data across all disks for improved performance, provides no redundancy (any single drive failure causes total data loss), and is suitable only when performance is prioritized over fault tolerance.
options: Requires a minimum of 2 drives to implement
Is also known as disk striping
Decreases reliability (failure of any disk in the array results in the loss of all data in the array)
Is also referred to as disk mirroring
Provides less usable capacity compared to RAID 1
Requires at least 3 drives to implement
Is suitable for systems where performance takes precedence over fault tolerance
Enhances reliability by duplicating data across all drives (failure of one drive does not result in data loss)
correctAnswer: Requires a minimum of 2 drives to implement
Is also known as disk striping
Decreases reliability (failure of any disk in the array results in the loss of all data in the array)
Is suitable for systems where performance takes precedence over fault tolerance

questionBank.stem: Hardware RAID Level 1: (Select 3 answers)
questionBank.explanation: RAID 1 (disk mirroring) requires at least 2 drives, duplicates all data on both drives so that if one fails the other continues operating, and provides fault tolerance at the cost of 50% usable disk space. It does not improve write performance since data must be written to both drives.
options: Requires at least 3 drives to implement
Is also known as disk striping
Requires at least 2 drives to implement
Improves reliability by duplicating data on each drive (if one drive fails, data remains accessible)
Is also referred to as disk mirroring
correctAnswer: Requires at least 2 drives to implement
Improves reliability by duplicating data on each drive (if one drive fails, data remains accessible)
Is also referred to as disk mirroring

questionBank.stem: Hardware RAID Level 5: (Select 3 answers)
questionBank.explanation: RAID 5 (striping with distributed parity) requires at least 3 drives, distributes parity information across all disks, and can tolerate a single drive failure without data loss by reconstructing missing data from parity. It offers both improved read performance and fault tolerance.
options: Requires at least 2 drives to implement
Can withstand the failure of more than one drive
Is also known as disk striping with double parity
Requires at least 3 drives to implement
Offers both increased performance and fault tolerance (a single drive failure does not result in data loss; the array can rebuild the missing data)
Requires at least 4 drives to implement
Is also known as disk striping with parity
correctAnswer: Requires at least 3 drives to implement
Offers both increased performance and fault tolerance (a single drive failure does not result in data loss; the array can rebuild the missing data)
Is also known as disk striping with parity

questionBank.stem: Hardware RAID Level 6: (Select 3 answers)
questionBank.explanation: RAID 6 (striping with double parity) requires at least 4 drives and uses two sets of distributed parity data across all disks, allowing it to tolerate up to 2 simultaneous drive failures without data loss. This provides greater fault tolerance than RAID 5 at the cost of additional disk overhead.
options: Is also known as disk striping with parity
Requires at least 4 drives to implement
Offers increased performance and fault tolerance (up to 2 drive failures can be tolerated without data loss)
Requires at least 3 drives to implement
Is also known as disk striping with double parity
Can continue operating after more than 2 drive failures
Requires at least 5 drives to implement
correctAnswer: Requires at least 4 drives to implement
Offers increased performance and fault tolerance (up to 2 drive failures can be tolerated without data loss)
Is also known as disk striping with double parity

questionBank.stem: Hardware RAID Level 10 (a.k.a. RAID 1+0): (Select 3 answers)
questionBank.explanation: RAID 10 (1+0) requires a minimum of 4 drives and combines RAID 1 mirroring with RAID 0 striping, creating a stripe of mirrored pairs. It can survive the failure of one drive in each mirrored pair, offering both excellent performance and fault tolerance with 50% disk overhead.
options: Requires a minimum of 4 drives to implement
Is known as a stripe of mirrors, combining RAID 1 (striping) with RAID 0 (mirroring)
Requires a minimum of 5 drives to implement
Offers increased performance and fault tolerance (the array can survive the failure of one drive in each mirrored pair)
Requires a minimum of 3 drives to implement
Can continue operating after more than 2 drive failures, regardless of which drives fail
Is known as a stripe of mirrors, combining RAID 1 (mirroring) with RAID 0 (striping)
correctAnswer: Requires a minimum of 4 drives to implement
Offers increased performance and fault tolerance (the array can survive the failure of one drive in each mirrored pair)
Is known as a stripe of mirrors, combining RAID 1 (mirroring) with RAID 0 (striping)

questionBank.stem: Which of the RAID levels listed below does not provide fault tolerance?
questionBank.explanation: RAID 0 is the only RAID level that provides no fault tolerance because it uses striping without any parity or mirroring. If any single disk in a RAID 0 array fails, all data across the entire array is lost.

questionBank.stem: In a configuration using the minimum required number of drives, which two of the following RAID levels provide the highest amount of usable storage space?
questionBank.explanation: Using the minimum required drives, RAID 0 (2 drives, total capacity = sum of all drives) and RAID 5 (3 drives, usable capacity = total minus one drive's worth for parity) both yield the same total usable capacity when calculated with equivalent drives. Both offer more usable space than RAID 1 (50% overhead) or RAID 10 (50% overhead).

questionBank.stem: Which of the RAID levels listed below provides the greatest level of redundancy?
questionBank.explanation: RAID 6 provides the greatest level of redundancy among standard RAID levels because it uses double distributed parity, allowing it to tolerate the simultaneous failure of up to 2 drives. RAID 5 only tolerates 1 drive failure, and RAID 1/10 can lose only 1 drive per mirrored pair.

questionBank.stem: Which of the following RAID levels offers the best performance?
questionBank.explanation: RAID 0 offers the best raw performance because it stripes data across all drives with zero overhead for parity calculations or mirroring. All disk capacity and I/O bandwidth are devoted entirely to performance, with no resources spent on redundancy.

questionBank.stem: Which of the answers listed below accurately describe(s) the characteristics of flash drives? (Select all that apply)
questionBank.explanation: USB flash drives are solid-state (no moving parts), non-volatile (retain data without power), rewritable storage devices designed for general-purpose file transfer and storage. They are plug-and-play across virtually all devices with USB ports, requiring no special drivers or configuration.
options: Plug-and-play across most devices supporting USB
Solid-state memory technology (containing no mechanical moving parts)
Primarily designed to expand storage capacity of compact electronics
Designed for general purpose file transfer and storage
Compatible with dedicated slots or card readers
correctAnswer: Plug-and-play across most devices supporting USB
Solid-state memory technology (containing no mechanical moving parts)
Designed for general purpose file transfer and storage

questionBank.stem: Shares Which of the following features differentiate memory cards from flash drives? (Select all that apply)
questionBank.explanation: Memory cards (SD, microSD, CF) differ from flash drives by being designed primarily to expand storage in compact electronics like cameras, smartphones, and tablets, and require dedicated card slots or external card readers rather than USB ports.
options: Compatible with dedicated slots or card readers
Primarily designed to expand storage capacity of compact electronics
Designed for general-purpose file transfer and storage
Solid-state memory technology (containing no mechanical moving parts)
Plug-and-play across most devices supporting USB
correctAnswer: Compatible with dedicated slots or card readers
Primarily designed to expand storage capacity of compact electronics

questionBank.stem: Due to space limitations, the shift to digital content, and the rise of faster storage alternatives, modern laptops no longer include a built-in version of this storage medium.
questionBank.explanation: Optical drives (CD/DVD/Blu-ray) have become increasingly rare in modern PCs due to the shift to digital content distribution, the rise of faster storage alternatives like USB flash drives and cloud storage, and the space constraints of thinner device designs.

questionBank.stem: What is the most common motherboard form factor used in desktop PCs?
questionBank.explanation: ATX (Advanced Technology eXtended) is the most common motherboard form factor for desktop PCs, measuring 12 × 9.6 inches with support for up to seven expansion slots. It is the standard that most full-size desktop cases and power supplies are designed to accommodate.

questionBank.stem: Which motherboard form factor would be the optimal choice for a compact or budget-friendly desktop build?
questionBank.explanation: Micro-ATX (mATX) is the optimal choice for compact or budget builds because it measures 9.6 × 9.6 inches — smaller than full ATX while still offering multiple expansion slots. It fits in both ATX and smaller mATX cases, providing a good balance of expandability and compact size.

questionBank.stem: Which of the answers listed below refers to a low-power consumption, small form factor motherboard type used in industrial and embedded PC applications?
questionBank.explanation: ITX (specifically Mini-ITX at 6.7 × 6.7 inches) is a low-power consumption, small form factor motherboard standard designed for compact systems. It is commonly used in small form factor PCs, HTPCs, and embedded systems where space and power efficiency are priorities.

questionBank.stem: Which of the following motherboard form factors is the smallest?
questionBank.explanation: ITX (Mini-ITX) is the smallest of the standard motherboard form factors at 6.7 × 6.7 inches, compared to Micro-ATX (9.6 × 9.6 inches) and full ATX (12 × 9.6 inches). Its compact size makes it ideal for space-constrained builds.

questionBank.stem: PCIe is a high-speed, serial expansion bus designed as a replacement for:
questionBank.explanation: PCIe (PCI Express) was designed as a high-speed, serial replacement for the older PCI (Peripheral Component Interconnect) parallel bus. PCIe uses point-to-point serial communication with dedicated lanes, offering significantly higher bandwidth than the shared PCI bus.

questionBank.stem: In PCIe architecture, a lane is a single, full-duplex, point-to-point serial communication path composed of two pairs of differential signaling wires, where one pair is used for transmitting data and the other pair for receiving data. The PCIe labeling (×1, ×4, ×8, ×12, ×16, and ×32) indicates the number of lanes available in an interface. The throughput of a single lane (as indicated by ×1) is determined by the specific PCIe generation and is typically measured in terms of gigatransfers per second (GT/s) or its equivalent bandwidth in MB/s. The multiplier (×) then provides a straightforward way to calculate the maximum theoretical aggregate bandwidth for the interface.
questionBank.explanation: In PCIe architecture, a lane is a single, full-duplex (simultaneous send and receive), point-to-point serial communication link between two components. PCIe slots are designated by the number of lanes (x1, x4, x8, x16), with each lane adding bandwidth.

questionBank.stem: Which of the answers listed below refers to the main power connector used in modern ATX power supplies?
questionBank.explanation: The 24-pin connector (P1) is the main power connector used on modern ATX motherboards, providing the primary power delivery from the PSU to the motherboard. It evolved from the original 20-pin ATX connector, with some PSUs offering a 20+4 pin adapter for backward compatibility.

questionBank.stem: Which of the following connectors provide(s) additional power to the CPU? (Select all that apply)
questionBank.explanation: The CPU receives additional power through dedicated connectors: the 4-pin 12V (also called P4 or ATX12V), the 8-pin 12V (EPS12V), or the 4+4-pin 12V connector (which can serve as either). These supplement the 24-pin main connector to provide the high current modern CPUs require.

questionBank.stem: Which of the answers listed below refer to auxiliary connector types most commonly used for supplying additional power to graphics cards? (Select 2 answers)
questionBank.explanation: The 6-pin and 8-pin PCIe power connectors are auxiliary connectors that provide additional power directly to high-performance graphics cards and other PCIe devices that require more power than the PCIe slot alone can supply (75W max from the slot).

questionBank.stem: Which motherboard connector features an L-shape design that prevents its improper insertion?
questionBank.explanation: SATA data connectors feature an L-shaped design (keyed connector) that prevents incorrect insertion, ensuring the cable can only be connected in the proper orientation. This prevents damage to the connector pins and ensures reliable connections.

questionBank.stem: Adding an eSATA device to a PC can be done either by attaching the device cable's connector directly to the motherboard's integrated I/O panel, plugging it in via eSATA port on a modular bracket mounted on the back of the PC case, or attaching it directly to a dedicated slot on the motherboard.
questionBank.explanation: The statement is false because adding an eSATA device requires an eSATA port — it cannot be connected to a standard USB port. eSATA uses a different connector and protocol than USB, requiring either a dedicated eSATA port on the motherboard's I/O panel or an eSATA expansion card/bracket.

questionBank.stem: Inside a PC case, connector cables from a power switch, reset switch, or LEDs on the front/top panel of the case attach to their corresponding slots located on the main power supply unit.
questionBank.explanation: The statement is false because front panel connector cables (power switch, reset switch, LEDs) connect to motherboard header pins, not to the PSU. These are low-voltage signal cables that connect to specific pin headers on the motherboard, and their polarity and position must be carefully matched using the motherboard manual.

questionBank.stem: The installation of USB ports located on the front panel of a computer case requires plugging in internal USB cable connectors into compatible groupings of metal pins (a.k.a. headers) on the motherboard.
questionBank.explanation: Front-panel USB ports connect to the motherboard via internal USB header pins using a cable from the case. This internal header connection allows the front USB ports to function through the motherboard's USB controller, providing convenient access without reaching the rear I/O panel.

questionBank.stem: Which of the following slots/ports on the PC motherboard enable(s) the connection of an M.2 device? (Select all that apply)
questionBank.explanation: M.2 slots use keying (B key, M key, or B+M key) to determine compatibility with SSDs. B key slots support SATA and PCIe x2 SSDs, M key slots support PCIe x4 (NVMe) SSDs, and B+M key slots provide broader compatibility. All three types enable M.2 SSD connectivity.

questionBank.stem: Motherboards used in laptops and mobile devices can be characterized by their proprietary design, which means that replacing a motherboard in such devices typically requires a part designed specifically for the make and model of the device.
questionBank.explanation: Laptop and mobile device motherboards are proprietary designs characterized by their compact size, integrated components (GPU, audio, networking built onto the board), and limited expandability compared to desktop motherboards. This integration is necessary to meet the space and power constraints of portable devices.

questionBank.stem: Which of the answers listed below refer to the main CPU manufacturers for personal computers? (Select 2 answers)
questionBank.explanation: Intel and AMD are the two primary CPU manufacturers for personal computers. Intel produces Core, Pentium, and Celeron lines for consumers and Xeon for servers, while AMD produces Ryzen for consumers and EPYC for servers.

questionBank.stem: High-end PC motherboards typically feature microprocessor sockets that are compatible with CPUs from different manufacturers.
questionBank.explanation: The statement is false because high-end PC motherboards typically feature a single CPU socket designed for one specific processor family. Multi-socket motherboards that support multiple CPUs are characteristic of server-class systems, not standard desktop PCs.

questionBank.stem: Which of the following answers refer to the characteristic features of a dedicated server motherboard? (Select 3 answers)
questionBank.explanation: Server-class motherboards are characterized by support for ECC RAM (for data integrity), multiple CPU sockets for increased processing power, and rack-mount or blade form factors designed for data center deployment. These features ensure reliability, scalability, and efficient space utilization.
options: Typically features a single CPU socket

questionBank.stem: Which of the answers listed below can be used to describe the characteristics of a typical desktop motherboard? (Select 3 answers)
questionBank.explanation: Desktop PC motherboards typically support non-ECC RAM (consumer-grade, less expensive), feature a single CPU socket, and are designed for tower case installation in standard ATX or mATX form factors. These characteristics reflect the consumer focus on cost-effectiveness and general-purpose computing.
options: Typically features a single CPU socket
correctAnswer: Typically features a single CPU socket

questionBank.stem: After completing initial diagnostics and allocating system resources, the startup BIOS program checks for information about secondary storage devices that might contain the OS. The list of these devices and the order in which they are checked can be found and configured in BIOS via:
questionBank.explanation: After POST diagnostics and resource allocation, the BIOS/UEFI firmware consults the boot options (boot order/boot priority) to determine which device to load the operating system from. This configurable list specifies the sequence of devices (HDD, SSD, USB, network/PXE) the system attempts to boot from.

questionBank.stem: Which BIOS configuration option helps mitigate a common vector for malware infection?
questionBank.explanation: USB permissions settings in BIOS/UEFI allow administrators to enable or disable USB ports, mitigating the risk of malware infection from unauthorized USB devices. Since USB drives are a common vector for malware, restricting USB access prevents users from introducing infected removable media.

questionBank.stem: The TPM functionality (if available) in the BIOS/UEFI setup interface provides which of the following features? (Select all that apply)
questionBank.explanation: TPM (Trusted Platform Module) provides comprehensive hardware-based security: it stores encryption keys securely for full-disk encryption, validates boot files through Secure Boot, logs boot processes to detect tampering, generates and stores cryptographic keys, and verifies system integrity for network access control. All these functions are performed in dedicated hardware, making them resistant to software-based attacks.
options: Allows only trusted boot files to run at startup
Stores encryption keys in secure hardware for full-disk encryption
Encrypts individual user accounts on the OS
Logs boot processes to detect changes
Safely creates and stores cryptographic keys
Checks system integrity before granting network access
correctAnswer: Allows only trusted boot files to run at startup
Stores encryption keys in secure hardware for full-disk encryption
Logs boot processes to detect changes
Safely creates and stores cryptographic keys
Checks system integrity before granting network access

questionBank.stem: Modern motherboards feature temperature sensors near key components like the CPU and chipset. The BIOS/UEFI firmware periodically polls these sensors to obtain current temperature readings and, according to the configured fan control settings (which can be automatic or user- defined), adjusts the speed of the system's cooling fans.
questionBank.explanation: Modern motherboards include temperature sensors near critical components (CPU, chipset, VRMs) to monitor heat levels in real-time. These sensors feed data to the BIOS/UEFI and OS monitoring tools, enabling automatic fan speed adjustments and thermal throttling to prevent overheating damage.

questionBank.stem: Shares Which of the following terms refers to the advanced security feature integrated into modern UEFI firmware that ensures only digitally signed, trusted software is allowed to run during the system’s startup process?
questionBank.explanation: Secure Boot is a UEFI feature that ensures only trusted, digitally signed bootloaders are allowed to execute during startup. The firmware verifies each bootloader's digital signature against pre-loaded keys, blocking any unsigned or modified boot code that could indicate malware.

questionBank.stem: Which of the answers listed below refer(s) to a boot password? (Select all that apply)
questionBank.explanation: A boot (user/system) password is required before the OS loads, primarily protecting against unauthorized use of the device. Unlike a BIOS/supervisor password, a boot password does not restrict access to BIOS/UEFI settings — it only prevents the system from completing the boot process without authentication.
options: Required to access and modify BIOS/UEFI settings
Primarily protects against unauthorized use of the device
Activated only when entering the BIOS configuration menu
Required before the OS loads to prevent unauthorized access
Does not restrict access to BIOS/UEFI settings
Prevents configuration changes to firmware settings
correctAnswer: Primarily protects against unauthorized use of the device
Required before the OS loads to prevent unauthorized access
Does not restrict access to BIOS/UEFI settings

questionBank.stem: Which of the following statements does not apply to a BIOS password?
questionBank.explanation: A BIOS (supervisor/administrator/setup) password protects access to the BIOS/UEFI setup program settings, not the system startup itself. The statement 'ensures that unauthorized users cannot start the system' describes a boot/user password, not a BIOS password.
options: Activated only when entering the BIOS configuration menu
Restricts access to the BIOS/UEFI setup interface
Does not interfere with the actual boot process once configured
Ensures that unauthorized users cannot start the system
Prevents unauthorized modifications to firmware settings
correctAnswer: Ensures that unauthorized users cannot start the system

questionBank.stem: A set of Intel CPU hardware enhancements that enable virtualization is known as:
questionBank.explanation: VT-x (Virtualization Technology for x86) is Intel's CPU hardware virtualization extension that enables efficient virtual machine execution. It allows hypervisors to run guest operating systems with near-native performance by providing hardware support for CPU virtualization operations.

questionBank.stem: Which of the answers listed below refers to AMD’s CPU hardware virtualization enhancements?
questionBank.explanation: AMD-V (AMD Virtualization) is AMD's implementation of CPU hardware virtualization extensions, equivalent to Intel's VT-x. It enables efficient hypervisor operation and guest OS execution on AMD processors.

questionBank.stem: Which of the following answers refer to the characteristic features of TPM? (Select 3 answers)
questionBank.explanation: TPM (Trusted Platform Module) is typically embedded directly into consumer device motherboards, provides security tied to a single specific device, and offers basic cryptographic functions including key storage and platform integrity verification. Unlike HSMs, TPM chips are not removable and are bound to the device they're installed in.
options: Supports multiple devices, users, and systems across a network, not tied to a single device
Can be a dedicated network-attached appliance, a PCIe card, or a USB device
Typically embedded directly into consumer devices (e.g., motherboards in PCs and laptops)
Designed for centralized cryptographic key management, supporting high volumes of cryptographic operations
Provides security that is specifically tied to a single device
Offers basic cryptographic functions, such as key storage and platform integrity support
correctAnswer: Typically embedded directly into consumer devices (e.g., motherboards in PCs and laptops)
Provides security that is specifically tied to a single device
Offers basic cryptographic functions, such as key storage and platform integrity support

questionBank.stem: Which of the answers listed below refer to HSM? (Select 3 answers)
questionBank.explanation: HSM (Hardware Security Module) is designed for centralized, high-volume cryptographic key management across multiple devices, users, and systems on a network. Unlike TPM, an HSM is not tied to a single device and can take the form of a network-attached appliance, PCIe card, or USB device.
options: Provides security that is specifically tied to a single device
Offers basic cryptographic functions, such as key storage and platform integrity support
Designed for centralized cryptographic key management, supporting high volumes of cryptographic operations
Supports multiple devices, users, and systems across a network, not tied to a single device
Typically embedded directly into consumer devices (e.g., motherboards in PCs and laptops)
Can be a dedicated network-attached appliance, a PCIe card, or a USB device
correctAnswer: Designed for centralized cryptographic key management, supporting high volumes of cryptographic operations
Supports multiple devices, users, and systems across a network, not tied to a single device
Can be a dedicated network-attached appliance, a PCIe card, or a USB device

questionBank.stem: Which of the following terms refers to a 32-bit CPU architecture?
questionBank.explanation: x86 refers to the 32-bit CPU architecture originally based on the Intel 8086 processor family. A 32-bit processor has a 32-bit address bus, limiting it to addressing a maximum of 4 GB of RAM.

questionBank.stem: Which of the terms listed below describes a CPU designed for 64-bit processing?
questionBank.explanation: x64 (also known as x86-64 or AMD64) describes a 64-bit CPU architecture that extends the original x86 instruction set to support 64-bit processing. It enables addressing far more than 4 GB of RAM and supports 64-bit operating systems and applications.

questionBank.stem: The presence of the Program Files (x86) folder on the C drive in MS Windows indicates that the system uses a 32-bit architecture and a 32-bit OS version.
questionBank.explanation: The statement is false because the presence of the 'Program Files (x86)' folder indicates a 64-bit version of Windows, not a 32-bit one. On 64-bit Windows, 32-bit applications are installed in 'Program Files (x86)' while 64-bit applications use the standard 'Program Files' folder. A 32-bit Windows installation has only one 'Program Files' folder.

questionBank.stem: A CPU design based on an instruction set that tries to improve speed by utilizing relatively few and simple instructions is called:
questionBank.explanation: RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computing) is a CPU architecture that uses a smaller, optimized set of simple instructions that each execute in a single clock cycle. This approach improves processing speed and efficiency compared to CISC (Complex Instruction Set Computing) architectures.

questionBank.stem: Which of the following answers refer(s) to ARM-type CPU architecture? (Select all that apply)
questionBank.explanation: ARM (Advanced RISC Machines) is a RISC-based CPU architecture characterized by low power consumption, a simplified instruction set for processing efficiency, and widespread use in mobile devices and embedded systems. Its energy efficiency makes it ideal for battery-powered devices like smartphones and tablets.
options: Typically used in personal computers, laptops, and servers
Focuses on simplifying the instruction set to enhance processing efficiency
Employs complex instructions for efficient memory management and backward compatibility
Commonly used in mobile devices and embedded systems
correctAnswer: Focuses on simplifying the instruction set to enhance processing efficiency
Commonly used in mobile devices and embedded systems

questionBank.stem: A type of CPU architecture where a single physical CPU contains more than one physical processing unit on a single integrated circuit is referred to as:
questionBank.explanation: Multicore architecture refers to a CPU design where a single physical processor chip contains multiple independent processing cores. Each core can execute instructions independently, enabling true parallel processing and improved multitasking performance.

questionBank.stem: The process of installing an expansion card should involve:
questionBank.explanation: Proper expansion card installation involves verifying compatibility with the motherboard slot, using ESD precautions, physically seating the card in the appropriate slot, securing it with a screw or latch, connecting any required power cables, and installing appropriate drivers. All of these steps should be performed for a successful installation.
options: Verifying hardware compatibility between the card and motherboard
Following ESD protection procedures during installation
Installing the latest drivers and software to ensure optimal functionality
Accessing the BIOS/UEFI settings to disable conflicting onboard hardware if necessary
Ensuring the system prioritizes the newly installed expansion card

questionBank.stem: Which of the actions listed below should be performed before the installation of a dedicated graphics card? (Select 3 answers)
questionBank.explanation: Before installing a GPU, you should verify the PSU meets the GPU's power requirements (wattage and correct power connectors), confirm the GPU is compatible with the motherboard's PCIe slot (typically PCIe x16), and check that the chassis has sufficient physical space and airflow for the card's size and cooling needs.
options: Check that the chassis has sufficient space and proper airflow for the GPU
Verify that the PSU meets the GPU’s power requirements (wattage and connector type)
Confirm that the GPU is compatible with the motherboard’s PCIe slot (typically PCIe x16)
Ensure that the GPU drivers are pre-installed on the system
Disable integrated graphics in the BIOS/UEFI settings before installation
Check for any pre-installed GPU software that might conflict with new drivers
correctAnswer: Check that the chassis has sufficient space and proper airflow for the GPU
Verify that the PSU meets the GPU’s power requirements (wattage and connector type)
Confirm that the GPU is compatible with the motherboard’s PCIe slot (typically PCIe x16)

questionBank.stem: A capture card is used for: (Select all that apply)
questionBank.explanation: A capture card is used for video input and audio input — it records or streams video and audio signals from external sources (game consoles, cameras, other PCs) by capturing the incoming A/V signal and saving it as a file or streaming it live. Unlike a graphics card which generates output, a capture card processes incoming signals.

questionBank.stem: Which type of adapter card enables Ethernet connectivity?
questionBank.explanation: A NIC (Network Interface Card) is the adapter card that provides Ethernet network connectivity to a computer. It connects to the network via an RJ-45 port and handles the data link and physical layer communication for wired LAN access.

questionBank.stem: Which of the following answers refer(s) to (a) solution(s) directly aimed at improving CPU heat dissipation? (Select all that apply)
questionBank.explanation: Thermal pads, CPU fans, heat sinks, thermal paste, and liquid-based cooling are all solutions directly aimed at improving CPU heat dissipation. Thermal paste fills microscopic gaps between the CPU and heat sink, the heat sink absorbs and disperses heat, fans provide active airflow, thermal pads offer an alternative to paste, and liquid cooling circulates coolant for maximum thermal transfer.

questionBank.stem: As opposed to active cooling components like cooling fans, heat sinks are considered passive cooling components because they do not require electrical power to operate.
questionBank.explanation: Heat sinks are considered passive cooling because they dissipate heat through thermal conduction and convection without any moving parts or power consumption. Active cooling components like fans require electrical power and use mechanical movement to force airflow over heated surfaces.

questionBank.stem: In CPU cooling, thermal paste is applied to fill the narrow gap between the:
questionBank.explanation: Thermal paste (also called thermal compound or thermal grease) is applied between the CPU and the heat sink to fill microscopic air gaps in the mating surfaces. Since air is a poor thermal conductor, the paste ensures efficient heat transfer from the CPU to the heat sink.

questionBank.stem: Which of the answers listed below refers to the standard voltage range for most residential and commercial power outlets in the United States?
questionBank.explanation: The standard voltage range for power outlets in North America (United States and Canada) is 110-120 VAC at 60 Hz. This is the voltage supplied by standard residential and commercial electrical outlets.

questionBank.stem: What is the standard voltage range used for power outlets in Europe?
questionBank.explanation: European countries use a standard power outlet voltage range of 220-240 VAC at 50 Hz, which is approximately double the North American voltage. This higher voltage allows for more efficient power transmission over longer distances.

questionBank.stem: A PSU's operation can be adjusted to the supplied voltage either by using a manual voltage selector on the back of the unit or automatically by the device. PSUs equipped with a manual voltage selector are referred to as fixed-input devices, while PSUs offering automatic voltage adjustment are known as auto-switching PSUs.
questionBank.explanation: Some PSUs include a manual voltage selector switch (110V/220V) on the back panel, while others have auto-sensing circuitry that automatically detects and adjusts to the input voltage. Modern PSUs increasingly use auto-switching to avoid damage from selecting the wrong voltage.

questionBank.stem: Which type of electric current is supplied to most of the internal PC components?
questionBank.explanation: The PSU converts alternating current (AC) from the wall outlet to direct current (DC) for internal PC components. Most internal components (CPU, RAM, drives, fans, motherboard circuits) require stable DC power at specific voltages (3.3V, 5V, 12V).

questionBank.stem: Which of the following PC components use circuits that operate at voltages up to 3.3V? (Select 2 answers)
questionBank.explanation: NVMe M.2 slots and RAM slots use circuits operating at 3.3V or lower. M.2 slots supply power over the bus at 3.3V, and modern DDR4/DDR5 RAM operates at 1.2V-1.5V, both well within the low-voltage range for sensitive digital components.

questionBank.stem: Shares Which of the PC components listed below operate on the 5V voltage rail?
questionBank.explanation: USB ports and devices operate on the 5V voltage rail provided by the PSU. The USB specification defines 5V as the standard bus voltage, which is why USB ports can charge devices and power peripherals at this voltage level.

questionBank.stem: Which of the following PC components typically draw power from the 12V voltage rail provided by the power supply? (Select 3 answers)
questionBank.explanation: The 12V voltage rail powers components with higher power demands: mechanical parts (case fans, HDD motors, optical drive motors), graphics cards, and PCIe expansion cards. The 12V rail is the most important in modern systems because CPUs and GPUs draw the majority of their power from it.
options: Mechanical parts (e.g., case fans, motors, actuators)
correctAnswer: Mechanical parts (e.g., case fans, motors, actuators)

questionBank.stem: Modern ATX motherboards use a 24-pin power connector. Some power supplies feature a 20+4- pin connector to maintain compatibility with both 20-pin and 24-pin motherboards. The 20+4 connector can be used fully assembled for 24-pin motherboards or with the 4-pin section left unattached for 20-pin motherboards.
questionBank.explanation: Some PSUs include a 20+4 pin detachable configuration on the main power connector, allowing compatibility with both older 20-pin and modern 24-pin ATX motherboards. The extra 4 pins can be separated or attached as needed for backward compatibility.

questionBank.stem: Which of the devices listed below would be required for a load-balancing setup where supplied power is split between multiple PSUs that automatically share the load and provide backup in case of a PSU failure?
questionBank.explanation: A redundant power supply (dual PSU) configuration is required for load-balancing setups where continuous uptime is critical. Redundant PSUs ensure that if one power supply fails, the other seamlessly takes over, preventing system downtime in enterprise and server environments.

questionBank.stem: In a modular power supply, the cables can be detached and reattached as needed, providing the flexibility to only use the cables required for the system, which helps reduce cable clutter and promotes better airflow within the computer case.
questionBank.explanation: A modular power supply allows cables to be detached and reattached as needed, so only the necessary cables are connected. This reduces cable clutter inside the chassis, improving airflow and cooling while simplifying cable management.

questionBank.stem: The power output rating of a PSU is measured in a unit known as:
questionBank.explanation: The power output rating of a PSU is measured in watts (W), which indicates the total amount of electrical power the unit can deliver to system components. When selecting a PSU, the wattage must exceed the combined power requirements of all installed components.

questionBank.stem: When selecting a PSU with energy efficiency in mind, the most important factor to consider is the 80 PLUS certification. This program rates PSUs based on their efficiency at various load levels, ensuring that they meet a minimum efficiency threshold. To maximize energy efficiency, reduce wasted energy, and lower long-term electricity costs, it is advisable to choose a PSU with a higher 80 PLUS rating, such as Gold, Platinum, or Titanium. These certifications indicate that the PSU operates more efficiently, reducing both energy loss and operational costs.
questionBank.explanation: When selecting an energy-efficient PSU, the 80 PLUS certification rating is the most important factor. The 80 PLUS program certifies PSUs that operate at a minimum of 80% efficiency, with higher tiers (Bronze, Silver, Gold, Platinum, Titanium) indicating greater efficiency and less wasted energy as heat.

questionBank.stem: Which of the following answers highlight key features that differentiate PCL from PostScript? (Select 3 answers)
questionBank.explanation: PCL (Printer Command Language) is generally more efficient for high-volume everyday printing, less suited for professional graphics than PostScript, and less demanding on printer memory and processing power. PCL is device-dependent and faster but produces less consistent results across different printer models.
options: Slower printing performance compared to PostScript due to complex processing
Generally more efficient for high-volume, everyday printing tasks than PostScript
Better suited for professional design, desktop publishing, and graphic arts than PostScript
Less suited for professional graphics or highly detailed printing tasks than PostScript
More resource-intensive than PostScript (requires more printer memory and processing power)
Less demanding on printer memory and processing power than PostScript
correctAnswer: Generally more efficient for high-volume, everyday printing tasks than PostScript
Less suited for professional graphics or highly detailed printing tasks than PostScript
Less demanding on printer memory and processing power than PostScript

questionBank.stem: Which of the answers listed below accurately describe PostScript? (Select 3 answers)
questionBank.explanation: PostScript has slower printing performance than PCL due to its complex rendering engine, is better suited for professional design and desktop publishing with its device-independent output, and is more resource-intensive requiring more printer memory and processing power for its precise page layout capabilities.
options: Less suited for professional graphics or highly detailed printing tasks than PCL
Slower printing performance compared to PCL due to complex processing
Better suited for professional design, desktop publishing, and graphic arts than PCL
Generally more efficient for high-volume, everyday printing tasks than PCL
Less demanding on printer memory and processing power than PCL
More resource-intensive than PCL (requires more printer memory and processing power)

Better suited for professional design, desktop publishing, and graphic arts than PCL
More resource-intensive than PCL (requires more printer memory and processing power)

questionBank.stem: Which of the following answers refers to software embedded within an MFD that provides basic instructions for its hardware to initialize and execute tasks?
questionBank.explanation: Firmware is the embedded software within a multifunction device (MFD) that provides its core operating instructions, controls hardware functions, and manages features like printing, scanning, and networking. It is stored in flash memory and can be updated to fix bugs or add features.

questionBank.stem: Which of the options listed below would typically be used to set up a direct, wired connection between an MFD and a single computer host?
questionBank.explanation: USB is the standard connectivity option for setting up a direct, wired connection between a single computer and a printer. A USB cable provides a simple, plug-and-play local connection without requiring network configuration.

questionBank.stem: Which connectivity option would be the most suitable in a scenario where multiple users on a wired network need access to MFD functions?
questionBank.explanation: Ethernet is the most suitable connectivity option when multiple users on a local area network need to share a single printer. Connecting the printer via Ethernet (RJ-45) to the network makes it accessible to all networked computers without requiring a dedicated PC to share it.

questionBank.stem: Which of the following answers refers to the most common wireless connectivity option for modern MFDs?
questionBank.explanation: 802.11x (Wi-Fi) is the most common wireless connectivity option for modern printers, allowing them to connect to the local wireless network. This enables any device on the same Wi-Fi network to send print jobs without physical cable connections.

questionBank.stem: Which of the answers listed below does not describe a disadvantage related to a printer share?
questionBank.explanation: The statement 'typically involves a higher cost and setup complexity' does not describe a disadvantage of a shared, network-connected printer — network printers actually reduce costs by allowing multiple users to share one device. The disadvantages of shared printers include network dependency, potential print queue congestion, and security concerns.
options: Each client computer needs to install the correct printer drivers for the shared printer
Only available when the host computer is turned on and connected to the network
Can become a bottleneck, especially with many users or large print jobs
Typically involves a higher cost and setup complexity
Offers limited control over user access, print quotas, and monitoring
If the host computer crashes or has issues, the printer becomes unavailable to everyone
correctAnswer: Typically involves a higher cost and setup complexity

questionBank.stem: Which of the following solutions would ensure the highest availability of the network printing service?
questionBank.explanation: A dedicated print server provides the highest availability for network printing resources by offloading print queue management from individual workstations. It manages print jobs centrally, ensuring reliable access to shared printers even when individual user PCs are powered off or busy.

questionBank.stem: A printer's capability to print on both sides of a paper sheet is referred to as duplex printing.
questionBank.explanation: Duplex printing refers to a printer's capability to print on both sides of a paper sheet, either automatically (auto-duplex) or manually (by re-feeding paper). This feature reduces paper consumption and is common in modern laser and inkjet printers.

questionBank.stem: Common printer configuration options include paper orientation settings that allow switching between Portrait mode (vertical layout) and Landscape mode (horizontal layout). Some printers may include additional orientation options, allowing the printout to be rotated by a specific degree. For most printers, the default paper orientation is Portrait mode.
questionBank.explanation: Paper orientation settings include portrait (vertical) and landscape (horizontal) modes, allowing users to configure the direction of their printout to match the document layout. These settings are configured through the printer driver or application print dialog.

questionBank.stem: Which printer setting allows configuration of a printout based on its paper size, type, or weight?
questionBank.explanation: Tray settings allow users to configure which paper tray to use for a print job, with each tray potentially holding different paper sizes (Letter, Legal, A4, etc.) or types (plain, glossy, envelope). This ensures the correct paper is selected for each print job.

questionBank.stem: Which print quality setting typically offers the lowest resolution, fastest print speed, and most efficient toner or ink usage?
questionBank.explanation: Draft mode offers the lowest resolution printing, using less ink or toner to produce output at the fastest speed. It is intended for preliminary document reviews where print quality is not critical, saving consumables and time.

questionBank.stem: Examples of security measures that can be implemented on a multifunction device or printer include:
questionBank.explanation: MFD security measures include user authentication (requiring login to use the device), secure print (holding jobs until the user authenticates at the device), audit logs (tracking usage), data encryption, and network access controls. All of these are valid security implementations for multifunction devices.
options: Login-based access via system software to ensure only authorized users can operate the device (user authentication)
Integrated ID card readers requiring users to authenticate using company-issued badges (badging)
Tracking of all printer activities, including user interactions, print jobs, and attempted access (audit logs)
PIN printing, requiring users to enter a numeric passcode before releasing print jobs (secured prints)

questionBank.stem: Which option allows an MFD to send a scanned document via an SMTP server?
questionBank.explanation: The email (scan to email) option allows an MFD to send scanned documents as email attachments via an SMTP server. The MFD must be configured with the SMTP server's IP address and authentication credentials to send emails directly from the device.

questionBank.stem: Which network scan service enables scanned documents to be saved directly to shared folders on a local network?
questionBank.explanation: SMB (Server Message Block) is the network protocol that enables scanned documents to be saved directly to shared network folders. The MFD is configured with the path to a file server and shared folder, and users must have write permissions to the share.

questionBank.stem: A user wants to scan a document from a multifunction printer and access it remotely from a personal online storage account. Which feature should be configured?
questionBank.explanation: Cloud services (such as OneDrive, Google Drive, or Dropbox) allow scanned documents to be uploaded to cloud storage, making them accessible remotely from any device with internet access. The MFD authenticates to the cloud service and uploads scans directly.

questionBank.stem: Which MFD/MFP component optimizes processing of multi-page documents?
questionBank.explanation: The ADF (Automatic Document Feeder) is the MFD/MFP component that optimizes processing of multi-page documents by automatically feeding pages over the scan head one at a time. This eliminates the need to manually place each page on the flatbed glass, significantly improving efficiency for batch scanning, copying, or faxing.

questionBank.stem: A flatbed scanner is a device that uses a flat glass surface on which documents, photos, or other materials are placed face down while a scanning mechanism moves underneath to capture the image.
